display_title: PR #50868: [XLA] Fix HLO parser crash when the wrapped op of a sugared async-start fails to parse

head_commit.message:
PR #50868: [XLA] Fix HLO parser crash when the wrapped op of a sugared async-start fails to parse

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/50868

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #49227.

Parsing a sugared async start like `call-start(), to_apply={%nope}` segfaults instead of returning a parse error. `CreateAsyncWrappedComputation` returns a null `HloComputation*` when the wrapped instruction fails to parse, and that null gets assigned into `std::optional<HloComputation*> async_computation`. Assigning a pointer engages the optional, so the `if (!async_computation)` check never fires and the null computation reaches `HloInstruction::CreateAsyncStart`, where the `HloAsyncStartInstruction` constructor dereferences it.

This regressed in 8bc8533fb6 (the refactor that introduced `CreateAsyncWrappedComputation`); before that the code checked the raw root pointer. The fix keeps the result in a local pointer and returns early when it is null, same as before the refactor. Any sugared `*-start` op was affected, for example `custom-call-start()` without `custom_call_target` crashed the same way.

## 🎯 Justification

Malformed HLO text should produce an `INVALID_ARGUMENT` status, not kill the process. `run_hlo_module`, `hlo-opt` and every test that parses HLO go through this code.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Two tests in `hlo_parser_test.cc`: `DesugarParsingTest_CallStart_InvalidToApply` (the input from the issue) and `DesugarParsingTest_CustomCallStart_MissingTarget` (different wrapped op, different failure). Both segfault at HEAD and pass with the fix.

```
bazel test //xla/hlo/parser:hlo_parser_test
```

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

None needed, the change is in the parser error path only.
Copybara import of the project:

--
1fb1a158018174cd70376db0a9d179d04abb513b by Stanislav Bardyuk <sbardyuk@google.com>:

[XLA] Fix HLO parser crash when a sugared async-start's wrapped op fails to parse

CreateAsyncWrappedComputation returns nullptr when the wrapped instruction
of a sugared async-start (call-start, custom-call-start, ...) fails to
parse. The result was assigned into std::optional<HloComputation*>, which
engages the optional even for nullptr, so the following null check never
fired and the null computation reached HloInstruction::CreateAsyncStart,
where HloAsyncStartInstruction's constructor dereferenced it (SIGSEGV).
Keep the raw pointer in a local and return early when it is null, as the
code did before 8bc8533fb6.

Fixes #49227.

Merging this change closes #50868

display_title: [XLA:GPU] Add GetDefaultCompilationPipeline in gpu_pipeline.

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Add GetDefaultCompilationPipeline in gpu_pipeline.

This change adds the gpu_pipeline library with GetDefaultCompilationPipeline.
The function returns the HLO pass pipeline of the GPU compiler as an
HloPipelineProto. For now, the proto has two sub-pipelines,
"annotate-host-compute" and "pre-spmd-partitioner". They have the same passes
and options as the first two pipelines of OptimizeHloModule.

OptimizeHloModule builds the proto and logs it at VLOG(1). It does not run
the proto yet. OptimizeHloModule still runs the passes with HloPassPipeline.

A new test creates each pass of the default pipeline from the pass registry.
The test makes sure that all pass names are registered and that each pass
reads all of its options. The test does not need a GPU.

The new gpu_pipeline_passes library links the HloPassRegistry registrations of
the passes in the pipeline. Only the test depends on it for now.

head_commit.message:
* Factor complex `Acosh` as `Log(x + Sqrt(x + one) * Sqrt(x - one))` to preserve the principal branch on $(-\infty, -1)$ and avoid `(x + 1) * (x - 1)` overflow.
* Use `Log1p(xm1 + Sqrt((x + one) * xm1))` for real inputs near $x \to 1^+$ (performance-neutral on TPU v5e).

display_title: PR #50406: [GPU] Preserve memory-space annotations in dynamic-slice fusions

head_commit.message:
PR #50406: [GPU] Preserve memory-space annotations in dynamic-slice fusions

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/50406

This fixes a case where dynamic-slice fusion can leave an FFI call’s buffers in ordinary memory even though the call requests collective (symmetric) memory, `S(7)`.

Consider this structure, with a 128-element `input` and 256-element `weights` and `destination` buffers. These are schematic HLO excerpts; the attribute names and indices are exact:

```text
tile = slice(weights, [128:256])
tmp = custom_call(input, tile),
      frontend_attributes={operands_memory_spaces="{0:7}",
                           results_memory_spaces="{0:7}"}
out = dynamic_update_slice(destination, tmp, 128)
```

The call requests collective memory for `input` and its result. Fusion replaces the temporary slices with views into their backing buffers:

```text
fused(p0_weights, p1_input, p2_destination) {
  tile = slice(p0_weights, [128:256])
  tmp = custom_call(p1_input, tile),
        frontend_attributes={operands_memory_spaces="{0:7}",
                             results_memory_spaces="{0:7}"}
  return dynamic_update_slice(p2_destination, tmp, 128)
}
```

Previously, the requirements remained only on the inner call, where allocation and boundary-copy analysis could miss them:

```text
out = fusion(weights, input, destination), calls=fused
```

This change puts the corresponding requirements on the outer fusion:

```text
out = fusion(weights, input, destination), calls=fused,
      frontend_attributes={operands_memory_spaces="{1:7,2:7}",
                           results_memory_spaces="{0:7}"}
```

The call’s operand `0` becomes fusion operand `1`. The destination at operand `2` also needs collective memory because the FFI now writes directly into its slice. `weights` stays in ordinary memory. Entry-boundary copies preserve ordinary-memory inputs and outputs where required.

The rewrite also preserves explicit input/output aliases. For example:

```text
tile = dynamic_slice(x, i)
updated = custom_call(tile, y)  // result aliases operand 0
out = dynamic_update_slice(x, updated, i)
```

This in-place update can fuse when the existing buffer and offset analysis proves that the aliased input and output refer to the same backing buffer and byte range. Mismatched regions, additional accesses sharing that backing buffer, or memory-space requirements that would conflict after fusion leave the call unfused.

Annotation handling is limited to custom calls and the `dynamic_slice_fusion` subtype.

Regression coverage includes operand reindexing, tuple outputs, update destinations, conflicting requests, O2 rollback, matching in-place updates, rejected overlaps, and shared collective allocation.
Copybara import of the project:

--
5ad0c53e46b3c8e34c1fb886b90a6b3059537f37 by Michael Goldfarb <mgoldfarb@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Preserve memory-space annotations in dynamic-slice fusions

Remap custom-call memory requirements to the fusion buffers that collective copy insertion and buffer assignment see. Preserve compatible slice fusions while declining merges that require conflicting memory spaces.

--
bbeb8973d395276434b991b02746b25064329191 by Michael Goldfarb <mgoldfarb@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Isolate the extended-offset annotation regression

Provide static slice configs directly so the regression exercises memory-space propagation while the fusion candidate is detached from its module.

--
7f32bc9803d43f81ae014d334c26029faedd950b by Michael Goldfarb <mgoldfarb@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Limit fusion memory annotations to dynamic-slice wrappers

Other fusion passes may inherit index-based frontend annotations without remapping their operands. Restrict buffer coloring and collective boundary-copy insertion to custom calls and recognized dynamic-slice fusions, with regressions for unrelated fusion kinds.

--
58e8f9ac2371e548f49f811ccdafc0896e99fa3c by Michael Goldfarb <mgoldfarb@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Preserve custom-call aliases across dynamic-slice fusion

Decline fusion when a captured slice or update changes an explicitly aliased custom-call buffer. Keep directly inferred aliases and cover shared collective allocation, tuple outputs, and operand restoration after rejected O2 rewrites.

--
ddc922ec7e3387414e139bbf628c62c84d6adf53 by Michael Goldfarb <mgoldfarb@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Allow matching aliased slice updates in dynamic-slice fusion

Use existing buffer mappings and offset configurations to preserve custom-call aliases when a slice is updated in place. Reject mismatched regions and additional accesses to the same backing buffer, and cover accepted fusion plus shared collective allocation.

--
bb4e31fbb3d80dd9d7dee12d0331b4ffc60ed81f by Michael Goldfarb <mgoldfarb@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Preserve frontend attributes when remapping fusion memory spaces

Apply remapped memory spaces after instruction replacement so unrelated frontend attributes retain their existing inheritance behavior. Remove inherited memory-space maps before merging to avoid stale indices, including when the remap is empty.

Cover direct custom-call replacement, DUS attribute precedence, empty memory-space maps, and tuple-result attribute preservation.

reads all of its options. The test does not need a GPU.

the passes in the pipeline. Only the test depends on it for now.

head_commit.message:
PR #47800: [XLA] Clamp out-of-bound set-dimension-size sizes in the HLO evaluator

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/47800

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47368.

`HloEvaluator::HandleSetDimensionSize` passes the raw runtime value of the
size operand straight into `MutableLiteralBase::SetDynamicSize`. Nothing
validates that value against the dimension bound, so a size larger than the
bound trips the fatal `CHECK_GE(bound, size)` in `literal.cc` and aborts the
whole process, and a negative size is silently stored and aborts later in
`LiteralBase::ToStatic` (`Shape::set_dimensions` CHECK). On the Interpreter
platform the evaluator executes the module directly, so a program whose
set-dimension-size size operand comes from input data can kill the process,
which is how the fuzzed module in the issue crashes `run_hlo_module`.

This change clamps the size to [0, bound] in `HandleSetDimensionSize` before
storing it. The evaluator is the only place a runtime program value becomes a
literal dynamic size, so this single site covers the crash class. In-contract
programs are unaffected (the clamp is the identity for sizes in [0, bound]).

Clamping (rather than erroring) matches the direction of #46625, which gives
the compiled CPU path the same [0, bound] clamp where the dynamic padder
materializes dynamic tensors, and keeps interpreter-vs-backend comparisons in
`run_hlo_module` executable for such modules (CPU/GPU execute them without
complaint today). Note that `get-dimension-size` still observes the raw size
value: it forwards the size-producing instruction's result, mirroring how the
dynamic padder forwards the raw size tensor on compiled backends, so only the
literal's stored dynamic size is clamped.

## 🎯 Justification

An out-of-contract runtime value in input data must not be able to abort the
process. The CHECKs themselves guard correct internal invariants (the literal
data buffer is sized to the bound); the evaluator is the boundary layer that
has to enforce the contract on program-provided sizes.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

- 🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Three regression tests in `hlo_evaluator_test.cc` next to the existing
`GetDimensionSize` test: `SetDimensionSizeClampsOversizedSize` (size
1851888704, the issue's value, expects dynamic size clamped to the bound 4),
`SetDimensionSizeClampsNegativeSize` (size -3, expects 0), and
`SetDimensionSizeKeepsSizeEqualToBound` (size 4, expects 4). Without the
fix the first aborts at `literal.cc` exactly like the issue and the second
observes the stored -3; with the fix all pass.
`bazel test //xla/hlo/evaluator/...` passes (331 tests in
`hlo_evaluator_test` plus the other evaluator targets).

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

The issue's StableHLO module and three minimal HLO variants (parameter size,
constant oversize, constant negative) now run cleanly under
`run_hlo_module --platform=Interpreter`; before the fix all four SIGABRT.
Copybara import of the project:

--

to MutableLiteralBase::SetDynamicSize. A size above the dimension bound

so program input data could kill it); a negative size is silently stored
and aborts later in LiteralBase::ToStatic. Clamp the size to [0, bound]

display_title: [XLA:CPU] Fix crash when a sort comparator calls nested computations

head_commit.message:
[XLA:CPU] Fix crash when a sort comparator calls nested computations

EmitSortComparator emitted the comparator without pre-emitting the
computations it transitively calls (a reduce's reducer, a map's mapper),
so EmitThreadLocalCall's FindOrDie(emitted_functions_, ...) aborted at
compile time for any comparator containing reduce, reduce-window, or
map. Pre-emit them via EmitNestedComputation, as the other kernel emit
paths already do.

Fixes #47366.

head_commit.message:
PR #48160: [XLA:CPU] Fix crash when a sort comparator calls nested computations

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48160

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47366.

Compiling a sort whose comparator contains a computation-calling op (reduce, reduce-window, map) crashes the CPU thunk emitter with `map_util.h:50 Check failed: it != collection.end() Map key not found`. `IrEmitter2::EmitSortComparator` emits the comparator directly with `EmitComputation`, so the computations the comparator transitively calls (for example a reduce's reducer) are never emitted, and the later `FindOrDie(emitted_functions_, ...)` lookup in `IrEmitter::EmitThreadLocalCall` dies.

This change pre-emits the comparator's transitively called computations through `IrEmitter::EmitNestedComputation` before emitting the comparator, the same way the other kernel emit paths already do (`IrEmitter2::EmitFusionHostKernel`, `ElementalKernelEmitter::ThreadLocalCallbackFactory`, `ComputationKernelEmitter`). `EmitNestedComputation` handles recursion and deduplicates through `emitted_functions_`, so comparators without called computations are unaffected.

## 🎯 Justification

The input is valid HLO: reduce/map inside a sort comparator is legal and the same modules run fine on the interpreter. The gap exists since the sort thunk emitter was introduced; simple elementwise comparators never hit it. With this change the reported module and several variants (reduce, reduce-window, map in the comparator) compile and run, and ordering-valid comparators match the interpreter reference.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

New `cpu_sort_test.cc` (CPU-only): a sort whose comparator calls a map and a reduce, with a deterministic input and exact expected output. Without the fix it crashes on the exact `Map key not found` CHECK; with the fix it passes. `//xla/service/cpu/tests/...`, `//xla/tests:sort_test_cpu` and `//xla/tests:topk_test_cpu` pass (the only failure, `cpu_vectorization_test`, fails identically at the base commit and is unrelated).

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

Ran the issue's original StableHLO module and three reduced HLO variants with `run_hlo_module` on CPU: no crashes; ordering-valid comparators match the interpreter reference exactly.
Copybara import of the project:

head_commit.message:
Pre-reserve containers and reuse InstructionVector in HloComputation::CloneInContext and HloInstruction::Defuse.

In `HloComputation::CloneInContext` (`xla/hlo/ir/hlo_computation.cc`), pre-reserve `postorder` and `visited` to `instruction_count()`, pre-reserve `instructions` to `postorder.size() + extra_parameters.size()`, and hoist `HloInstruction::InstructionVector new_operands` outside the instruction loop with `new_operands.clear()`. In `HloInstruction::Defuse` (`xla/hlo/ir/hlo_instruction.cc`), pre-reserve `defused_instructions` to `fused_computation->instruction_count()` and hoist `InstructionVector new_operands` outside the post-order loop with `new_operands.clear()`.

Microbenchmark results (`--benchmark_repetitions=9`, `-c opt`):

| Benchmark | Baseline | Optimized | Delta |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `BM_CloneComputation/16` | 37,222 ns | 33,199 ns | -10.8% (1.12x) |
| `BM_CloneComputation/1024` | 2,302,569 ns | 2,013,412 ns | -12.6% (1.14x) |
| `BM_Defuse/16` | 15,541 ns | 12,092 ns | -22.2% (1.29x) |
| `BM_Defuse/1024` | 1,281,447 ns | 1,113,105 ns | -13.1% (1.15x) |

head_commit.message:
PR #47800: [XLA] Clamp out-of-bound set-dimension-size sizes in the HLO evaluator

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/47800

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47368.

`HloEvaluator::HandleSetDimensionSize` passes the raw runtime value of the
size operand straight into `MutableLiteralBase::SetDynamicSize`. Nothing
validates that value against the dimension bound, so a size larger than the
bound trips the fatal `CHECK_GE(bound, size)` in `literal.cc` and aborts the
whole process, and a negative size is silently stored and aborts later in
`LiteralBase::ToStatic` (`Shape::set_dimensions` CHECK). On the Interpreter
platform the evaluator executes the module directly, so a program whose
set-dimension-size size operand comes from input data can kill the process,
which is how the fuzzed module in the issue crashes `run_hlo_module`.

This change clamps the size to [0, bound] in `HandleSetDimensionSize` before
storing it. The evaluator is the only place a runtime program value becomes a
literal dynamic size, so this single site covers the crash class. In-contract
programs are unaffected (the clamp is the identity for sizes in [0, bound]).

Clamping (rather than erroring) matches the direction of #46625, which gives
the compiled CPU path the same [0, bound] clamp where the dynamic padder
materializes dynamic tensors, and keeps interpreter-vs-backend comparisons in
`run_hlo_module` executable for such modules (CPU/GPU execute them without
complaint today). Note that `get-dimension-size` still observes the raw size
value: it forwards the size-producing instruction's result, mirroring how the
dynamic padder forwards the raw size tensor on compiled backends, so only the
literal's stored dynamic size is clamped.

## 🎯 Justification

An out-of-contract runtime value in input data must not be able to abort the
process. The CHECKs themselves guard correct internal invariants (the literal
data buffer is sized to the bound); the evaluator is the boundary layer that
has to enforce the contract on program-provided sizes.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

- 🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Three regression tests in `hlo_evaluator_test.cc` next to the existing
`GetDimensionSize` test: `SetDimensionSizeClampsOversizedSize` (size
1851888704, the issue's value, expects dynamic size clamped to the bound 4),
`SetDimensionSizeClampsNegativeSize` (size -3, expects 0), and
`SetDimensionSizeKeepsSizeEqualToBound` (size 4, expects 4). Without the
fix the first aborts at `literal.cc` exactly like the issue and the second
observes the stored -3; with the fix all pass.
`bazel test //xla/hlo/evaluator/...` passes (331 tests in
`hlo_evaluator_test` plus the other evaluator targets).

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

The issue's StableHLO module and three minimal HLO variants (parameter size,
constant oversize, constant negative) now run cleanly under
`run_hlo_module --platform=Interpreter`; before the fix all four SIGABRT.
Copybara import of the project:

--

[XLA] Clamp out-of-bound set-dimension-size sizes in the HLO evaluator

HloEvaluator::HandleSetDimensionSize passed the raw runtime size operand
to MutableLiteralBase::SetDynamicSize. A size above the dimension bound
trips the fatal CHECK_GE(bound, size) in literal.cc and aborts the

and aborts later in LiteralBase::ToStatic. Clamp the size to [0, bound]

head_commit.message:
PR #46783: [XLA] Simplify binary concatenate of a repeated operand to a broadcast

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/46783

#ai-generated

`HandleConcatenate` returns early for a two-operand concatenate whose operands are not a broadcasted scalar. That early return sits above the `Concat(X, X, ...)` to broadcast-of-reshape rewrite, so the rewrite fires for three or more operands and never for exactly two.

This is issue #26780. The five-operand form is simplified:

```
ENTRY main {
  x = s8[2,1,4] parameter(0)
  ROOT concat = s8[2,5,4] concatenate(x, x, x, x, x), dimensions={1}
}
```

while the two-operand form is left alone:

```
ENTRY main {
  x = s8[3,1,4] parameter(0)
  ROOT concat = s8[3,2,4] concatenate(x, x), dimensions={1}
}
```

A concatenate materializes its result, a broadcast of a reshape does not and fuses into its consumer, so the two-operand case pays for a copy that the three-or-more case avoids. Doubling a degenerate dimension is a common shape after a reshape or an expand_dims, so the gap is easy to hit.

The fix guards the concat-to-pad rewrite with its scalar-broadcast condition instead of returning from the function, so the two-operand case falls through to the existing degenerate-dimension check. Precedence is unchanged: a two-operand concatenate with a broadcasted scalar operand still becomes a pad. Most of the diff is the reindentation that guard causes.

Verification: I did not build XLA for this change, so the argument is by reading. The new `BinaryConcatToBroadcast` test mirrors the existing `ConcatToBroadcast` test with two operands instead of six, and the touched lines are clang-format clean.

head_commit.message:
PR #48378: [XLA:CPU] Do not send reductions with non-trivial reducers to YNNPACK

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48378

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn` only looked at the root of the reducer computation (`add`/`max`/`min` of the two parameters). If the reducer has any other instructions in it, for example a side-effecting outfeed like in the module from #47374, the reduce still got wrapped into a `__ynn_fusion`. The YNN emitter then hits `CHECK_EQ(reduce_instr->to_apply()->instruction_count(), 3)` in `DefineReduceOp` when the YNN executable is built on the first execution, so compile succeeds and the process aborts at run time. For `reduce-window` there is no CHECK and the extra instructions were just dropped.

This change makes the matcher require the reducer to be exactly the two parameters plus the root, which is the shape the emitter can actually express (same guard as in `all_reduce_key.cc`, `all_reduce_combiner.cc` etc.). Such reductions now take the regular CPU path instead.

Added two tests to `library_rewriter_test.cc` that run `LibraryRewriter` on a `reduce` and a `reduce-window` with an outfeed in the reducer and check that no YNN fusion is created. Both fail before this change.

Note that the module from the issue still does not compile on CPU after this change: it now hits the `computation_partitioner.cc:269` CHECK in the MLIR fusion emitter, which is the same crash site as #47373 and not YNN-specific.

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #47374. Process abort at run time on valid (if unusual) HLO with default flags.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

`bazel test //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:ynn_matcher_test_cpu //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:library_rewriter_test //xla/backends/cpu/tests:ynn_fusion_test_cpu`

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

None (CPU only, covered by the unit tests above).
Copybara import of the project:

--

[XLA:CPU] Do not send reductions with non-trivial reducers to YNNPACK

IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn only matched the root of the reducer
computation, so a reduce whose reducer contains extra instructions (for
example an outfeed) was wrapped into a __ynn_fusion. The YNN emitter can
only express the reducer root and CHECKs instruction_count() == 3 when the
executable is built on first execution, so the process aborted at run
time; for reduce-window the extra instructions were silently dropped.

Require the reducer to be exactly the two parameters plus the root before
claiming a reduce or reduce-window for YNNPACK.

Fixes #47374.

Merging this change closes #48378

head_commit.message:
PR #48160: [XLA:CPU] Fix crash when a sort comparator calls nested computations

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48160

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47366.

Compiling a sort whose comparator contains a computation-calling op (reduce, reduce-window, map) crashes the CPU thunk emitter with `map_util.h:50 Check failed: it != collection.end() Map key not found`. `IrEmitter2::EmitSortComparator` emits the comparator directly with `EmitComputation`, so the computations the comparator transitively calls (for example a reduce's reducer) are never emitted, and the later `FindOrDie(emitted_functions_, ...)` lookup in `IrEmitter::EmitThreadLocalCall` dies.

This change pre-emits the comparator's transitively called computations through `IrEmitter::EmitNestedComputation` before emitting the comparator, the same way the other kernel emit paths already do (`IrEmitter2::EmitFusionHostKernel`, `ElementalKernelEmitter::ThreadLocalCallbackFactory`, `ComputationKernelEmitter`). `EmitNestedComputation` handles recursion and deduplicates through `emitted_functions_`, so comparators without called computations are unaffected.

## 🎯 Justification

The input is valid HLO: reduce/map inside a sort comparator is legal and the same modules run fine on the interpreter. The gap exists since the sort thunk emitter was introduced; simple elementwise comparators never hit it. With this change the reported module and several variants (reduce, reduce-window, map in the comparator) compile and run, and ordering-valid comparators match the interpreter reference.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

New `cpu_sort_test.cc` (CPU-only): a sort whose comparator calls a map and a reduce, with a deterministic input and exact expected output. Without the fix it crashes on the exact `Map key not found` CHECK; with the fix it passes. `//xla/service/cpu/tests/...`, `//xla/tests:sort_test_cpu` and `//xla/tests:topk_test_cpu` pass (the only failure, `cpu_vectorization_test`, fails identically at the base commit and is unrelated).

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

Ran the issue's original StableHLO module and three reduced HLO variants with `run_hlo_module` on CPU: no crashes; ordering-valid comparators match the interpreter reference exactly.

display_title: Make SubgraphConverter::EmitInstruction iterative for all ops

head_commit.message:
Make SubgraphConverter::EmitInstruction iterative for all ops

`SubgraphConverter::EmitInstruction` only used an iterative worklist for elementwise ops. Non-elementwise ops like `bitcast`, `transpose`, `reshape` and `slice` still recursed through `HloToMlir` and the operand provider, which costs a few KiB of stack per op. So a long enough chain of these ops inside a single fusion overflows the stack of the compiling thread. (We've seen fusions with chains of a few hundred bitcasts when `algsimp` is disabled.)

Therefore this change computes the operand indices when an instruction gets pushed onto the work stack and emits all in-subgraph operands iteratively before lowering the instruction itself. Ops with dedicated emitters (`concatenate`, `reduce`, `gather`, `pad`, etc.) still request their operands through the operand provider like before.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 1005369296

head_commit.message:
PR #50868: [XLA] Fix HLO parser crash when the wrapped op of a sugared async-start fails to parse

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/50868

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #49227.

Parsing a sugared async start like `call-start(), to_apply={%nope}` segfaults instead of returning a parse error. `CreateAsyncWrappedComputation` returns a null `HloComputation*` when the wrapped instruction fails to parse, and that null gets assigned into `std::optional<HloComputation*> async_computation`. Assigning a pointer engages the optional, so the `if (!async_computation)` check never fires and the null computation reaches `HloInstruction::CreateAsyncStart`, where the `HloAsyncStartInstruction` constructor dereferences it.

This regressed in 8bc8533fb6 (the refactor that introduced `CreateAsyncWrappedComputation`); before that the code checked the raw root pointer. The fix keeps the result in a local pointer and returns early when it is null, same as before the refactor. Any sugared `*-start` op was affected, for example `custom-call-start()` without `custom_call_target` crashed the same way.

## 🎯 Justification

Malformed HLO text should produce an `INVALID_ARGUMENT` status, not kill the process. `run_hlo_module`, `hlo-opt` and every test that parses HLO go through this code.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Two tests in `hlo_parser_test.cc`: `DesugarParsingTest_CallStart_InvalidToApply` (the input from the issue) and `DesugarParsingTest_CustomCallStart_MissingTarget` (different wrapped op, different failure). Both segfault at HEAD and pass with the fix.

```
bazel test //xla/hlo/parser:hlo_parser_test
```

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

None needed, the change is in the parser error path only.
Copybara import of the project:

--

[XLA] Fix HLO parser crash when a sugared async-start's wrapped op fails to parse

head_commit.message:
PR #47800: [XLA] Clamp out-of-bound set-dimension-size sizes in the HLO evaluator

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/47800

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47368.

`HloEvaluator::HandleSetDimensionSize` passes the raw runtime value of the
size operand straight into `MutableLiteralBase::SetDynamicSize`. Nothing
validates that value against the dimension bound, so a size larger than the
bound trips the fatal `CHECK_GE(bound, size)` in `literal.cc` and aborts the
whole process, and a negative size is silently stored and aborts later in
`LiteralBase::ToStatic` (`Shape::set_dimensions` CHECK). On the Interpreter
platform the evaluator executes the module directly, so a program whose
set-dimension-size size operand comes from input data can kill the process,
which is how the fuzzed module in the issue crashes `run_hlo_module`.

This change clamps the size to [0, bound] in `HandleSetDimensionSize` before
storing it. The evaluator is the only place a runtime program value becomes a
literal dynamic size, so this single site covers the crash class. In-contract
programs are unaffected (the clamp is the identity for sizes in [0, bound]).

Clamping (rather than erroring) matches the direction of #46625, which gives
the compiled CPU path the same [0, bound] clamp where the dynamic padder
materializes dynamic tensors, and keeps interpreter-vs-backend comparisons in
`run_hlo_module` executable for such modules (CPU/GPU execute them without
complaint today). Note that `get-dimension-size` still observes the raw size
value: it forwards the size-producing instruction's result, mirroring how the
dynamic padder forwards the raw size tensor on compiled backends, so only the
literal's stored dynamic size is clamped.

## 🎯 Justification

An out-of-contract runtime value in input data must not be able to abort the
process. The CHECKs themselves guard correct internal invariants (the literal
data buffer is sized to the bound); the evaluator is the boundary layer that
has to enforce the contract on program-provided sizes.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

- 🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Three regression tests in `hlo_evaluator_test.cc` next to the existing
`GetDimensionSize` test: `SetDimensionSizeClampsOversizedSize` (size
1851888704, the issue's value, expects dynamic size clamped to the bound 4),
`SetDimensionSizeClampsNegativeSize` (size -3, expects 0), and
`SetDimensionSizeKeepsSizeEqualToBound` (size 4, expects 4). Without the
fix the first aborts at `literal.cc` exactly like the issue and the second
observes the stored -3; with the fix all pass.
`bazel test //xla/hlo/evaluator/...` passes (331 tests in
`hlo_evaluator_test` plus the other evaluator targets).

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

The issue's StableHLO module and three minimal HLO variants (parameter size,
constant oversize, constant negative) now run cleanly under
`run_hlo_module --platform=Interpreter`; before the fix all four SIGABRT.

head_commit.message:
PR #50868: [XLA] Fix HLO parser crash when the wrapped op of a sugared async-start fails to parse

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/50868

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #49227.

Parsing a sugared async start like `call-start(), to_apply={%nope}` segfaults instead of returning a parse error. `CreateAsyncWrappedComputation` returns a null `HloComputation*` when the wrapped instruction fails to parse, and that null gets assigned into `std::optional<HloComputation*> async_computation`. Assigning a pointer engages the optional, so the `if (!async_computation)` check never fires and the null computation reaches `HloInstruction::CreateAsyncStart`, where the `HloAsyncStartInstruction` constructor dereferences it.

This regressed in 8bc8533fb6 (the refactor that introduced `CreateAsyncWrappedComputation`); before that the code checked the raw root pointer. The fix keeps the result in a local pointer and returns early when it is null, same as before the refactor. Any sugared `*-start` op was affected, for example `custom-call-start()` without `custom_call_target` crashed the same way.

## 🎯 Justification

Malformed HLO text should produce an `INVALID_ARGUMENT` status, not kill the process. `run_hlo_module`, `hlo-opt` and every test that parses HLO go through this code.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Two tests in `hlo_parser_test.cc`: `DesugarParsingTest_CallStart_InvalidToApply` (the input from the issue) and `DesugarParsingTest_CustomCallStart_MissingTarget` (different wrapped op, different failure). Both segfault at HEAD and pass with the fix.

```
bazel test //xla/hlo/parser:hlo_parser_test
```

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

None needed, the change is in the parser error path only.
Copybara import of the project:

[XLA] Fix HLO parser crash when a sugared async-start's wrapped op fails to parse

CreateAsyncWrappedComputation returns nullptr when the wrapped instruction
of a sugared async-start (call-start, custom-call-start, ...) fails to
parse. The result was assigned into std::optional<HloComputation*>, which
engages the optional even for nullptr, so the following null check never
fired and the null computation reached HloInstruction::CreateAsyncStart,
where HloAsyncStartInstruction's constructor dereferenced it (SIGSEGV).
Keep the raw pointer in a local and return early when it is null, as the
code did before 8bc8533fb6.

Fixes #49227.

Merging this change closes #50868

head_commit.message:
PR #47800: [XLA] Clamp out-of-bound set-dimension-size sizes in the HLO evaluator

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/47800

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47368.

`HloEvaluator::HandleSetDimensionSize` passes the raw runtime value of the
size operand straight into `MutableLiteralBase::SetDynamicSize`. Nothing
validates that value against the dimension bound, so a size larger than the
bound trips the fatal `CHECK_GE(bound, size)` in `literal.cc` and aborts the
whole process, and a negative size is silently stored and aborts later in
`LiteralBase::ToStatic` (`Shape::set_dimensions` CHECK). On the Interpreter
platform the evaluator executes the module directly, so a program whose
set-dimension-size size operand comes from input data can kill the process,
which is how the fuzzed module in the issue crashes `run_hlo_module`.

This change clamps the size to [0, bound] in `HandleSetDimensionSize` before
storing it. The evaluator is the only place a runtime program value becomes a
literal dynamic size, so this single site covers the crash class. In-contract
programs are unaffected (the clamp is the identity for sizes in [0, bound]).

Clamping (rather than erroring) matches the direction of #46625, which gives
the compiled CPU path the same [0, bound] clamp where the dynamic padder
materializes dynamic tensors, and keeps interpreter-vs-backend comparisons in
`run_hlo_module` executable for such modules (CPU/GPU execute them without
complaint today). Note that `get-dimension-size` still observes the raw size
value: it forwards the size-producing instruction's result, mirroring how the
dynamic padder forwards the raw size tensor on compiled backends, so only the
literal's stored dynamic size is clamped.

## 🎯 Justification

An out-of-contract runtime value in input data must not be able to abort the
process. The CHECKs themselves guard correct internal invariants (the literal
data buffer is sized to the bound); the evaluator is the boundary layer that
has to enforce the contract on program-provided sizes.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

- 🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Three regression tests in `hlo_evaluator_test.cc` next to the existing
`GetDimensionSize` test: `SetDimensionSizeClampsOversizedSize` (size
1851888704, the issue's value, expects dynamic size clamped to the bound 4),
`SetDimensionSizeClampsNegativeSize` (size -3, expects 0), and
`SetDimensionSizeKeepsSizeEqualToBound` (size 4, expects 4). Without the
fix the first aborts at `literal.cc` exactly like the issue and the second
observes the stored -3; with the fix all pass.
`bazel test //xla/hlo/evaluator/...` passes (331 tests in
`hlo_evaluator_test` plus the other evaluator targets).

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

The issue's StableHLO module and three minimal HLO variants (parameter size,
constant oversize, constant negative) now run cleanly under
`run_hlo_module --platform=Interpreter`; before the fix all four SIGABRT.
Copybara import of the project:

--
9fc7ccd3dc0ef41d1a215b8866f281bb130f4e27 by Stanislav Bardyuk <sbardyuk@google.com>:

[XLA] Clamp out-of-bound set-dimension-size sizes in the HLO evaluator

HloEvaluator::HandleSetDimensionSize passed the raw runtime size operand
to MutableLiteralBase::SetDynamicSize. A size above the dimension bound
trips the fatal CHECK_GE(bound, size) in literal.cc and aborts the
process (the Interpreter platform executes modules with the evaluator,
so program input data could kill it); a negative size is silently stored
and aborts later in LiteralBase::ToStatic. Clamp the size to [0, bound]
at this single point, matching the clamp #46625 gives the compiled CPU
path. In-contract programs are unaffected.

Fixes #47368.

Merging this change closes #47800

display_title: Pre-reserve containers and reuse InstructionVector in HloComputation::CloneInContext and HloInstruction::Defuse.

head_commit.message:
Pre-reserve containers and reuse InstructionVector in HloComputation::CloneInContext and HloInstruction::Defuse.

In `HloComputation::CloneInContext` (`xla/hlo/ir/hlo_computation.cc`), pre-reserve `postorder` and `visited` to `instruction_count()`, pre-reserve `instructions` to `postorder.size() + extra_parameters.size()`, and hoist `HloInstruction::InstructionVector new_operands` outside the instruction loop with `new_operands.clear()`. In `HloInstruction::Defuse` (`xla/hlo/ir/hlo_instruction.cc`), pre-reserve `defused_instructions` to `fused_computation->instruction_count()` and hoist `InstructionVector new_operands` outside the post-order loop with `new_operands.clear()`.

Microbenchmark results (`--benchmark_repetitions=9`, `-c opt`):

head_commit.message:
PR #48378: [XLA:CPU] Do not send reductions with non-trivial reducers to YNNPACK

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48378

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn` only looked at the root of the reducer computation (`add`/`max`/`min` of the two parameters). If the reducer has any other instructions in it, for example a side-effecting outfeed like in the module from #47374, the reduce still got wrapped into a `__ynn_fusion`. The YNN emitter then hits `CHECK_EQ(reduce_instr->to_apply()->instruction_count(), 3)` in `DefineReduceOp` when the YNN executable is built on the first execution, so compile succeeds and the process aborts at run time. For `reduce-window` there is no CHECK and the extra instructions were just dropped.

This change makes the matcher require the reducer to be exactly the two parameters plus the root, which is the shape the emitter can actually express (same guard as in `all_reduce_key.cc`, `all_reduce_combiner.cc` etc.). Such reductions now take the regular CPU path instead.

Added two tests to `library_rewriter_test.cc` that run `LibraryRewriter` on a `reduce` and a `reduce-window` with an outfeed in the reducer and check that no YNN fusion is created. Both fail before this change.

Note that the module from the issue still does not compile on CPU after this change: it now hits the `computation_partitioner.cc:269` CHECK in the MLIR fusion emitter, which is the same crash site as #47373 and not YNN-specific.

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #47374. Process abort at run time on valid (if unusual) HLO with default flags.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

`bazel test //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:ynn_matcher_test_cpu //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:library_rewriter_test //xla/backends/cpu/tests:ynn_fusion_test_cpu`

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

None (CPU only, covered by the unit tests above).
Copybara import of the project:

[XLA:CPU] Do not send reductions with non-trivial reducers to YNNPACK

IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn only matched the root of the reducer
computation, so a reduce whose reducer contains extra instructions (for
example an outfeed) was wrapped into a __ynn_fusion. The YNN emitter can
only express the reducer root and CHECKs instruction_count() == 3 when the
executable is built on first execution, so the process aborted at run
time; for reduce-window the extra instructions were silently dropped.

Require the reducer to be exactly the two parameters plus the root before
claiming a reduce or reduce-window for YNNPACK.

Fixes #47374.

Merging this change closes #48378

display_title: Add GPU executable load micro-benchmarks

head_commit.message:
Add GPU executable load micro-benchmarks

None of our existing GPU benchmarks measures how long it takes to load a serialized executable or how much host memory a loaded executable keeps alive. We want to reduce the host-side cost of loading AOT compiled GPU executables, so we need a baseline first.

This change adds `BM_LoadSerializedExecutable` (PjRt `LoadSerializedExecutable`) and `BM_GpuAotFromSerializedAndLoad` (deserializing the AOT compilation result and loading it into an `Executable`, below the PjRt layer) to `//xla/pjrt/gpu:se_gpu_pjrt_client_benchmark_test`. `BM_HloModuleFromProto` measures only the creation of the optimized `HloModule` from its proto plus its fingerprint, which is an upper bound of what we can save by not materializing the module. `BM_FirstExecuteAfterLoad` and `BM_ExecuteAfterDeserialize` cover the first and the steady state executions after loading. The destruction of the loaded objects is not part of the measured time.

All of them except `BM_ExecuteAfterDeserialize` also report the heap bytes retained by one result (for `BM_FirstExecuteAfterLoad` after the first execution) as a `heap_bytes_retained` counter. This counter is based on `mallinfo`, so it's only reported with glibc.

The benchmarks run on a tiny module, a synthetic chain of 500 dots and two real models from `xla/tools/benchmarks/hlo` (Gemma4 2B and a MaxText train step). The execution benchmarks use zero-initialized arguments and skip the MaxText module since it donates its arguments. The H100 variant now runs on a full GPU since the Gemma4 arguments don't fit into a MIG partition.

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Add a pass to convert an emitted kernel into a callable function.

Add the `VirtualizeSubKernelPass` MLIR pass that operates on `llvm` + `nvvm` modules. The pass:
1. Strips trailing scratch pointer arguments from Triton modules.
2. Appends `rel_bid_i32` to the entry signature.
3. Virtualizes `ctaid.{x,y,z}`, `nctaid.{x,y,z}`, `tid.{x,y,z}`, and `ntid.{x,y,z}` (delinearizing 2D/3D grids and thread blocks).
4. Rewrites 0-operand `nvvm.barrier` ops to partial-CTA `bar.sync 0, N` when the sub-kernel uses fewer threads than `max_threads`.
5. Packs shared memory globals into 16-byte-aligned byte offsets of external `@global_smem` and records "xla.shared_memory_bytes" attribute.

head_commit.message:
PR #49580: [XLA:CPU] Allow fusing into kReduceWindow

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49580

📝 Summary of Changes
#ai_generated (but it's been in use internally for several weeks)

When XLA:CPU reduces a large array, it first splits the reduction into a reduce-window that produces partial sums and a smaller reduce over those. The fusion pass knows how to *fuse producers into a reduce*, but not into a *reduce-window*. So in something like `sum(x * y)`, the multiply generates its own loop and writes its entire result to memory, which is read immediately after by the reduce (instead of performing a more optimal loop fusion).

The actual fix is adding `kReduceWindow` to `CanBeLoopFused`, which is one line. I also had to teach `ReusesOperandElements` that a reduce-window with non-overlapping windows touches each input element only once, *as is already done for reduce*.

🎯 Justification

This affects every large reduction that doesn't go to YNNPACK. I ran into it while looking into #49131.

🚀 Kind of Contribution

⚡️ Performance Improvement

📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

```
ENTRY main {
  x = bf16[64,1048576] parameter(0)
  y = bf16[64,1048576] parameter(1)
  m = bf16[64,1048576] multiply(x, y)
  c = bf16[] constant(0)
  ROOT r = bf16[64] reduce(m, c), dimensions={1}, to_apply=add
}
```

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| bf16 (above) | 78.0 ms | 28.8 ms |
| same in s32 | 77.7 ms | 12.7 ms |

I didn't see any changes outside the noise on the other CPU benchmarks.

🧪 Unit Tests:

New tests in `hlo_instruction_test` check that a reduce-window reuses elements only when its windows overlap. In `cpu_instruction_fusion_test`, one test fuses a multiply into a non-overlapping reduce-window and another checks that `exp` stays out of an overlapping one.

There was also an existing test in `cpu_fusion_test` that used reduce-window as its example of an op that can't be fused, which is no longer true, so I switched it to sort.

head_commit.message:
PR #46783: [XLA] Simplify binary concatenate of a repeated operand to a broadcast

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/46783

#ai-generated

`HandleConcatenate` returns early for a two-operand concatenate whose operands are not a broadcasted scalar. That early return sits above the `Concat(X, X, ...)` to broadcast-of-reshape rewrite, so the rewrite fires for three or more operands and never for exactly two.

This is issue #26780. The five-operand form is simplified:

```
ENTRY main {
  x = s8[2,1,4] parameter(0)
  ROOT concat = s8[2,5,4] concatenate(x, x, x, x, x), dimensions={1}
}
```

while the two-operand form is left alone:

```
ENTRY main {
  x = s8[3,1,4] parameter(0)
  ROOT concat = s8[3,2,4] concatenate(x, x), dimensions={1}
}
```

A concatenate materializes its result, a broadcast of a reshape does not and fuses into its consumer, so the two-operand case pays for a copy that the three-or-more case avoids. Doubling a degenerate dimension is a common shape after a reshape or an expand_dims, so the gap is easy to hit.

The fix guards the concat-to-pad rewrite with its scalar-broadcast condition instead of returning from the function, so the two-operand case falls through to the existing degenerate-dimension check. Precedence is unchanged: a two-operand concatenate with a broadcasted scalar operand still becomes a pad. Most of the diff is the reindentation that guard causes.

Verification: I did not build XLA for this change, so the argument is by reading. The new `BinaryConcatToBroadcast` test mirrors the existing `ConcatToBroadcast` test with two operands instead of six, and the touched lines are clang-format clean.

Copybara import of the project:

[XLA] Simplify binary concatenate of a repeated operand to a broadcast

HandleConcatenate returns early for a two-operand concatenate whose
operands are not a broadcasted scalar, which shadows the later
Concat(X, X, ...) to broadcast-of-reshape rewrite. The rewrite therefore
fires for three or more operands but never for exactly two.

Guard the concat-to-pad rewrite with the scalar-broadcast condition
instead of returning, so the two-operand case reaches the existing
degenerate-dimension check. Rewrite precedence is unchanged: a binary
concatenate with a broadcasted scalar operand still becomes a pad.

head_commit.message:
PR #48160: [XLA:CPU] Fix crash when a sort comparator calls nested computations

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48160

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47366.

Compiling a sort whose comparator contains a computation-calling op (reduce, reduce-window, map) crashes the CPU thunk emitter with `map_util.h:50 Check failed: it != collection.end() Map key not found`. `IrEmitter2::EmitSortComparator` emits the comparator directly with `EmitComputation`, so the computations the comparator transitively calls (for example a reduce's reducer) are never emitted, and the later `FindOrDie(emitted_functions_, ...)` lookup in `IrEmitter::EmitThreadLocalCall` dies.

This change pre-emits the comparator's transitively called computations through `IrEmitter::EmitNestedComputation` before emitting the comparator, the same way the other kernel emit paths already do (`IrEmitter2::EmitFusionHostKernel`, `ElementalKernelEmitter::ThreadLocalCallbackFactory`, `ComputationKernelEmitter`). `EmitNestedComputation` handles recursion and deduplicates through `emitted_functions_`, so comparators without called computations are unaffected.

## 🎯 Justification

The input is valid HLO: reduce/map inside a sort comparator is legal and the same modules run fine on the interpreter. The gap exists since the sort thunk emitter was introduced; simple elementwise comparators never hit it. With this change the reported module and several variants (reduce, reduce-window, map in the comparator) compile and run, and ordering-valid comparators match the interpreter reference.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

New `cpu_sort_test.cc` (CPU-only): a sort whose comparator calls a map and a reduce, with a deterministic input and exact expected output. Without the fix it crashes on the exact `Map key not found` CHECK; with the fix it passes. `//xla/service/cpu/tests/...`, `//xla/tests:sort_test_cpu` and `//xla/tests:topk_test_cpu` pass (the only failure, `cpu_vectorization_test`, fails identically at the base commit and is unrelated).

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

Ran the issue's original StableHLO module and three reduced HLO variants with `run_hlo_module` on CPU: no crashes; ordering-valid comparators match the interpreter reference exactly.
Copybara import of the project:

--

[XLA:CPU] Fix crash when a sort comparator calls nested computations

EmitSortComparator emitted the comparator without pre-emitting the
computations it transitively calls (a reduce's reducer, a map's mapper),
so EmitThreadLocalCall's FindOrDie(emitted_functions_, ...) aborted at
compile time for any comparator containing reduce, reduce-window, or
map. Pre-emit them via EmitNestedComputation, as the other kernel emit
paths already do.

Fixes #47366.

display_title: Reject deserialization of early-exit GPU executables

head_commit.message:
Reject deserialization of early-exit GPU executables

For executables compiled with `xla_early_exit_with_layouts`, `StreamExecutorExecutable::SerializeExecutable` only writes the compile options. `StreamExecutorExecutable::Deserialize` turned that back into an executable without a `CompiledModule`, which hits the `CHECK` in the constructor that requires an `HloModule`. So loading such a serialized executable crashed the process.

Loading early-exit executables isn't supported anyway (`CommonPjRtClient::LoadInternal` rejects them), so `Deserialize` now returns an `InvalidArgument` error instead of crashing. Serializing early-exit compilations stays as is.

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Support bit-width-changing bitcast-convert in the dynamic padder

Same-width bitcast-converts already pass through ChooseIdentityValue via
the elementwise exit, but bit-width-changing ones are not elementwise and
hit the Unimplemented default, failing compilation for e.g. tf.bitcast
applied to the dynamically-sized output of tf.where (issue #45967).
Padding data reinterprets to padding data and the minor dimension the op
adds or removes is static, so no identity value is needed.

Also make InferBitcastConvertShape reject a dynamic consumed minor
dimension for the narrowing form, so that ill-defined case keeps failing
loudly instead of compiling to garbage values.

head_commit.message:
PR #46793: [XLA] Support bit-width-changing bitcast-convert in the dynamic padder

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/46793

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #45967.

The dynamic padder failed with "Unimplemented padding for instruction:
bitcast-convert" whenever a bit-width-changing bitcast-convert consumed an
operand with a dynamic dimension. Same-width bitcast-converts already worked
through the elementwise early-exit in ChooseIdentityValue, but the
width-changing form is not elementwise (its shape changes), so it fell
through to the unimplemented default.

Padding data reinterprets to padding data under a bitcast, and the dimension
the op adds or removes is always the static innermost one, so no identity
value is needed. This adds kBitcastConvert to the group of ops that return
nullptr from ChooseIdentityValue. Dynamic dimension inference already
propagates the dynamic dimensions correctly for both directions (it routes
bitcast-convert through the index-preserving elementwise passthrough, and
pre-existing dimensions keep their indices in both the widening and the
narrowing form).

The repro from the issue is tf.bitcast applied to the output of tf.where:
where produces s64[<=16,1], and the int64 to float32 bitcast makes
f32[<=16,1,2], which then failed to compile.

One hole is closed on the way: shape inference checked only the bound of the
minor dimension consumed by a narrowing bitcast-convert, so a dynamic minor
dimension (for example f32[10,<=2] to s64[10]) was accepted, and with the
padder fix such an ill-defined program would have compiled and produced
garbage instead of failing. InferBitcastConvertShape now rejects a dynamic
consumed minor dimension explicitly.

## 🎯 Justification

Eager TF executes the where + bitcast graph fine; XLA refused to compile it.
The graph is well defined for any runtime size, so this is a missing case in
the dynamic padder, not a semantic limitation.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Two pass-level regression tests in dynamic_padder_test.cc (widening
s64[<=16,1] -> f32[<=16,1,2] and narrowing f32[<=16,2] -> s64[<=16]); both
fail with the exact issue error before the fix and pass after. Two shape
inference tests cover the narrowing form: dynamic major dimension accepted,
dynamic consumed minor dimension rejected.

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

Two execution tests in the same file check the computed values end to end
with a dynamic dimension present (s64 -> s32 widening and s32 -> s64
narrowing with known bit patterns). Run on CPU.

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Skip block-scaled and sparse dots in DotDecomposer

DotDecomposer rebuilds non-canonical dots from lhs and rhs only. For dots
with extra operands this drops block_scaling_config and the scale
operands, silently producing an unscaled dot that passes the verifier.
For sparse dots it drops sparsity_config, and the result fails
verification on contracting dimension sizes.

Skip dots with more than two operands, as transpose_folding and
batch_dot_simplification already do.

head_commit.message:
PR #49899: [XLA:CPU] Do not offload reduce-window with base dilation to YNNPACK

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49899

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn` checked `base_dilation` only for window dimensions with `size > 1` or `stride > 1`. A dimension with window size 1 and stride 1 but `base_dilation = 2` passed the check, and `DefineReduceWindowOp` in the YNNPACK emitter never looks at base dilation, so it computed the undilated reduction and wrote it into the (larger) dilated output buffer. Silent wrong result, no error.

This change moves the base dilation check in front of the `size > 1 || stride > 1` block so it applies to every window dimension. Such reduce-windows now stay on the regular CPU emitter, which handles base dilation correctly. The window dilation and window reversal checks stay where they were, both are no-ops on a size 1 window.

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #48714. `LIBRARY_FUSION_TYPE_REDUCE` is enabled by default, so any CPU `reduce-window` with `lhs_dilate` on a size 1 / stride 1 dimension and at least 4096 elements returned wrong values. Reachable from plain `lax.reduce_window(..., base_dilation=...)` in JAX.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

- `YnnReduceTest.ReduceWindowWithBaseDilationIsNotFused` in `xla/backends/cpu/transforms/ynn_matcher_test.cc` compiles the module from the issue (`f32[64,128]`, `window={size=2x1 stride=2x1 lhs_dilate=1x2}`, max), checks that no `__ynn_fusion` is created, and compares the result against the interpreter with an exact error spec. The fixture gets the interpreter reference mixin for that.

Fails without the fix (fusion present, 8159 of 8160 elements wrong) and passes with it:

```
bazel test //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:ynn_matcher_test_cpu //xla/backends/cpu/tests:ynn_fusion_test_cpu //xla/tests:reduce_window_test_cpu
```

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

The new test runs the module on CPU and compares with the interpreter. The existing YNNPACK fusion and reduce-window test targets above still pass.

IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn only checked base_dilation for window
dimensions with size > 1 or stride > 1. A size-1, stride-1 dimension with
base_dilation > 1 passed the check, and DefineReduceWindowOp does not
implement base dilation, so the YNNPACK path returned the undilated result
in the dilated output shape. Check base_dilation on every window dimension

head_commit.message:
PR #49899: [XLA:CPU] Do not offload reduce-window with base dilation to YNNPACK

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49899

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn` checked `base_dilation` only for window dimensions with `size > 1` or `stride > 1`. A dimension with window size 1 and stride 1 but `base_dilation = 2` passed the check, and `DefineReduceWindowOp` in the YNNPACK emitter never looks at base dilation, so it computed the undilated reduction and wrote it into the (larger) dilated output buffer. Silent wrong result, no error.

This change moves the base dilation check in front of the `size > 1 || stride > 1` block so it applies to every window dimension. Such reduce-windows now stay on the regular CPU emitter, which handles base dilation correctly. The window dilation and window reversal checks stay where they were, both are no-ops on a size 1 window.

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #48714. `LIBRARY_FUSION_TYPE_REDUCE` is enabled by default, so any CPU `reduce-window` with `lhs_dilate` on a size 1 / stride 1 dimension and at least 4096 elements returned wrong values. Reachable from plain `lax.reduce_window(..., base_dilation=...)` in JAX.

🐛 Bug Fix

- `YnnReduceTest.ReduceWindowWithBaseDilationIsNotFused` in `xla/backends/cpu/transforms/ynn_matcher_test.cc` compiles the module from the issue (`f32[64,128]`, `window={size=2x1 stride=2x1 lhs_dilate=1x2}`, max), checks that no `__ynn_fusion` is created, and compares the result against the interpreter with an exact error spec. The fixture gets the interpreter reference mixin for that.

Fails without the fix (fusion present, 8159 of 8160 elements wrong) and passes with it:


Don't require an HloModule for RunAsync VLOGs

PjRtStreamExecutorRawLoadedExecutable::Execute logs the module name before and after RunAsync via `Executable::module()`, which CHECK-fails when the executable doesn't hold an HloModule. So turning on `VLOG(1)` crashes the GPU execute path for such executables.

display_title: Own constant content when the HloModule is not embedded

head_commit.message:
Own constant content when the HloModule is not embedded

Non-scalar constants are not emitted as initializers in the LLVM IR. Instead the executable keeps their content and copies it to the device on the first execution. That content is a `DenseDataIntermediate` which aliases the literal of the constant instruction in the HloModule. With `CompileOptions::embed_hlo_module=false`, `GpuCompiler::RunBackend` doesn't move the module into the `GpuExecutable`, so the module (and with it the literal) gets destroyed at the end of `RunBackend` and the constants point to freed memory. This went unnoticed so far because the only users of that option (the autotuner and the Triton numerics verifier) compile clones that share their literals with a source module that stays alive.

So this change makes the constants own a copy of their content in `RunBackend`, but only if the module doesn't get embedded. I made the decision there because that's the place that decides to drop the module. The default path (module embedded) keeps aliasing the literals, so there is no extra copy and no additional memory use. The new `DenseDataIntermediate::ToOwned()` only copies aliased data, so sub-byte constants (which are already packed into an owned buffer) don't get copied a second time.

There are two new tests in `xla/service/gpu/gpu_compiler_test.cc`. The first one compiles a module with an f32 and an s4 constant without embedding it, makes sure the module is gone, and then checks the constant contents and the result of an execution. Without the fix it reports a heap-use-after-free under ASAN. The second one doesn't need ASAN: it checks that the constant content aliases the module's literal if and only if the module gets embedded, which also pins the no-copy behavior of the default path.

display_title: PR #46783: [XLA] Simplify binary concatenate of a repeated operand to a broadcast

head_commit.message:
PR #46783: [XLA] Simplify binary concatenate of a repeated operand to a broadcast

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/46783

#ai-generated

`HandleConcatenate` returns early for a two-operand concatenate whose operands are not a broadcasted scalar. That early return sits above the `Concat(X, X, ...)` to broadcast-of-reshape rewrite, so the rewrite fires for three or more operands and never for exactly two.

This is issue #26780. The five-operand form is simplified:

```
ENTRY main {
  x = s8[2,1,4] parameter(0)
  ROOT concat = s8[2,5,4] concatenate(x, x, x, x, x), dimensions={1}
}
```

while the two-operand form is left alone:

```
ENTRY main {
  x = s8[3,1,4] parameter(0)
  ROOT concat = s8[3,2,4] concatenate(x, x), dimensions={1}
}
```

A concatenate materializes its result, a broadcast of a reshape does not and fuses into its consumer, so the two-operand case pays for a copy that the three-or-more case avoids. Doubling a degenerate dimension is a common shape after a reshape or an expand_dims, so the gap is easy to hit.

The fix guards the concat-to-pad rewrite with its scalar-broadcast condition instead of returning from the function, so the two-operand case falls through to the existing degenerate-dimension check. Precedence is unchanged: a two-operand concatenate with a broadcasted scalar operand still becomes a pad. Most of the diff is the reindentation that guard causes.

Verification: I did not build XLA for this change, so the argument is by reading. The new `BinaryConcatToBroadcast` test mirrors the existing `ConcatToBroadcast` test with two operands instead of six, and the touched lines are clang-format clean.

display_title: PR #48875: [XLA] Fix trivial reduce-window simplification with negative window padding

head_commit.message:
PR #48875: [XLA] Fix trivial reduce-window simplification with negative window padding

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48875

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`AlgebraicSimplifier` rewrites a `reduce-window` with a 1x...x1 window (no stride, dilation or reversal, add/min/max reducer) into a plain elementwise op on the operand, wrapped in a `pad` when the window has padding. The wrapper was only built when some padding amount was positive. Window padding can also be negative (a crop), which changes the shape just like positive padding does. With only negative padding the rewrite replaced a `f32[7,4]` reduce-window with a `f32[8,4]` add, `ReplaceInstruction` failed its shape RET_CHECK, and the simplifier turned that into a fatal CHECK, so compilation aborted the process.

This change applies the positive padding amounts with a `pad` and the negative amounts with a `slice`, so the replacement always has the reduce-window's shape. It deliberately never emits a `pad` with negative edge padding: such a pad would be seen by consumers later in the same simplifier sweep, and the pad-into-reduce-window / pad-into-convolution folds in this file assume non-negative edge padding, so a crop feeding a padded reduce-window would have been folded into a wrong net padding (#48715 covers that fold). The mixed-sign case, which previously produced a negative pad and relied on `HandlePad` to turn it into a slice, now takes the same pad-plus-slice path. For the module from the issue the whole thing simplifies to `slice(x)`.

Tests added to `algebraic_simplifier_test.cc`: `TrivialReduceWindowWithNegativePad` (aborts the test binary before this change), `TrivialReduceWindowWithMixedSignPad`, and `TrivialReduceWindowWithNegativePadFeedingPaddedReduceWindow` (checks the consumer keeps its own padding).

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #48719. Compile-time process abort on valid HLO (negative reduce-window padding is documented and reachable from `lax.reduce_window`). The pass is shared by all backends.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

`bazel test //xla/hlo/transforms/simplifiers:algebraic_simplifier_test`

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

None added (pass-level fix). Verified locally on CPU that the issue's module and the crop-feeding-a-padded-reduce-window module compile and produce the expected values.

head_commit.message:
PR #48378: [XLA:CPU] Do not send reductions with non-trivial reducers to YNNPACK

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48378

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn` only looked at the root of the reducer computation (`add`/`max`/`min` of the two parameters). If the reducer has any other instructions in it, for example a side-effecting outfeed like in the module from #47374, the reduce still got wrapped into a `__ynn_fusion`. The YNN emitter then hits `CHECK_EQ(reduce_instr->to_apply()->instruction_count(), 3)` in `DefineReduceOp` when the YNN executable is built on the first execution, so compile succeeds and the process aborts at run time. For `reduce-window` there is no CHECK and the extra instructions were just dropped.

This change makes the matcher require the reducer to be exactly the two parameters plus the root, which is the shape the emitter can actually express (same guard as in `all_reduce_key.cc`, `all_reduce_combiner.cc` etc.). Such reductions now take the regular CPU path instead.

Added two tests to `library_rewriter_test.cc` that run `LibraryRewriter` on a `reduce` and a `reduce-window` with an outfeed in the reducer and check that no YNN fusion is created. Both fail before this change.

Note that the module from the issue still does not compile on CPU after this change: it now hits the `computation_partitioner.cc:269` CHECK in the MLIR fusion emitter, which is the same crash site as #47373 and not YNN-specific.

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #47374. Process abort at run time on valid (if unusual) HLO with default flags.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

`bazel test //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:ynn_matcher_test_cpu //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:library_rewriter_test //xla/backends/cpu/tests:ynn_fusion_test_cpu`

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

None (CPU only, covered by the unit tests above).

[XLA:CPU] Do not send reductions with non-trivial reducers to YNNPACK

IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn only matched the root of the reducer
computation, so a reduce whose reducer contains extra instructions (for
example an outfeed) was wrapped into a __ynn_fusion. The YNN emitter can
only express the reducer root and CHECKs instruction_count() == 3 when the
executable is built on first execution, so the process aborted at run
time; for reduce-window the extra instructions were silently dropped.

Require the reducer to be exactly the two parameters plus the root before
claiming a reduce or reduce-window for YNNPACK.

head_commit.message:
PR #48378: [XLA:CPU] Do not send reductions with non-trivial reducers to YNNPACK

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48378

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn` only looked at the root of the reducer computation (`add`/`max`/`min` of the two parameters). If the reducer has any other instructions in it, for example a side-effecting outfeed like in the module from #47374, the reduce still got wrapped into a `__ynn_fusion`. The YNN emitter then hits `CHECK_EQ(reduce_instr->to_apply()->instruction_count(), 3)` in `DefineReduceOp` when the YNN executable is built on the first execution, so compile succeeds and the process aborts at run time. For `reduce-window` there is no CHECK and the extra instructions were just dropped.

This change makes the matcher require the reducer to be exactly the two parameters plus the root, which is the shape the emitter can actually express (same guard as in `all_reduce_key.cc`, `all_reduce_combiner.cc` etc.). Such reductions now take the regular CPU path instead.

Added two tests to `library_rewriter_test.cc` that run `LibraryRewriter` on a `reduce` and a `reduce-window` with an outfeed in the reducer and check that no YNN fusion is created. Both fail before this change.

Note that the module from the issue still does not compile on CPU after this change: it now hits the `computation_partitioner.cc:269` CHECK in the MLIR fusion emitter, which is the same crash site as #47373 and not YNN-specific.

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #47374. Process abort at run time on valid (if unusual) HLO with default flags.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

`bazel test //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:ynn_matcher_test_cpu //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:library_rewriter_test //xla/backends/cpu/tests:ynn_fusion_test_cpu`

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

None (CPU only, covered by the unit tests above).

display_title: Add DumpHloSnapshotIfEnabled overload without HloModule

head_commit.message:
Add DumpHloSnapshotIfEnabled overload without HloModule

To decide whether to dump an HLO snapshot and to name the file, `DumpHloSnapshotIfEnabled` only needs the module's unique id, its name and its `DebugOptions`. The snapshot content itself comes from the executable's `HloProto`, so the `HloModule` isn't needed at all.

This change adds an overload that takes just these three values, so callers can dump snapshots without having an `HloModule` around. We will need that once executables materialize their module lazily (a follow-up switches `Service` and `Executable::dumping_snapshot` over to it).

The existing `HloModule` overload now delegates to the new one, so the behavior and the file names don't change.

display_title: Support GPU AOT results without an embedded HLO module

head_commit.message:
Support GPU AOT results without an embedded HLO module

A `GpuExecutable` compiled without an embedded HLO module serializes to a `GpuExecutableProto` without `hlo_module_with_config.hlo_module`, but such a proto can't be turned into a `GpuAotCompilationResult` and loaded again. `GpuAotCompilationResult::FromProto` and `FromSerialized` always deserialize the module, which fails on the missing field. On top of that the split proto writer always creates an empty `hlo_module_with_config.hlo_module` (while normalizing backend configs and clearing the module id), so the reader can't tell anymore that there is no module.

Therefore this change makes the split writer, `GpuAotCompilationResult` and `GpuExecutable::FromProto` check for the inner `hlo_module` and only touch or deserialize the module if it's present. This also covers config-only protos, where `hlo_module_with_config` only has the `config` set. (`optimized_module()` is already nullable, and `GpuExecutable::FromProto` already handled a missing `hlo_module_with_config`.) Without a module, `GetCompiledMemoryStats` now computes the padded peak from the buffer assignment alone and reports the unpadded peak as 0 (unknown), and the `LoadExecutable` VLOG no longer dereferences a null module. Output and behaviour for executables with an embedded module are unchanged.

Note that this only fixes newly written artifacts. Module-less artifacts written by the old split writer contain an empty `hlo_module` and still fail to load, as they did before.

head_commit.message:
PR #46793: [XLA] Support bit-width-changing bitcast-convert in the dynamic padder

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/46793

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #45967.

The dynamic padder failed with "Unimplemented padding for instruction:
bitcast-convert" whenever a bit-width-changing bitcast-convert consumed an
operand with a dynamic dimension. Same-width bitcast-converts already worked
through the elementwise early-exit in ChooseIdentityValue, but the
width-changing form is not elementwise (its shape changes), so it fell
through to the unimplemented default.

Padding data reinterprets to padding data under a bitcast, and the dimension
the op adds or removes is always the static innermost one, so no identity
value is needed. This adds kBitcastConvert to the group of ops that return
nullptr from ChooseIdentityValue. Dynamic dimension inference already
propagates the dynamic dimensions correctly for both directions (it routes
bitcast-convert through the index-preserving elementwise passthrough, and
pre-existing dimensions keep their indices in both the widening and the
narrowing form).

The repro from the issue is tf.bitcast applied to the output of tf.where:
where produces s64[<=16,1], and the int64 to float32 bitcast makes
f32[<=16,1,2], which then failed to compile.

One hole is closed on the way: shape inference checked only the bound of the
minor dimension consumed by a narrowing bitcast-convert, so a dynamic minor
dimension (for example f32[10,<=2] to s64[10]) was accepted, and with the
padder fix such an ill-defined program would have compiled and produced
garbage instead of failing. InferBitcastConvertShape now rejects a dynamic
consumed minor dimension explicitly.

## 🎯 Justification

Eager TF executes the where + bitcast graph fine; XLA refused to compile it.
The graph is well defined for any runtime size, so this is a missing case in
the dynamic padder, not a semantic limitation.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Two pass-level regression tests in dynamic_padder_test.cc (widening
s64[<=16,1] -> f32[<=16,1,2] and narrowing f32[<=16,2] -> s64[<=16]); both
fail with the exact issue error before the fix and pass after. Two shape
inference tests cover the narrowing form: dynamic major dimension accepted,
dynamic consumed minor dimension rejected.

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

Two execution tests in the same file check the computed values end to end
with a dynamic dimension present (s64 -> s32 widening and s32 -> s64
narrowing with known bit patterns). Run on CPU.

head_commit.message:
PR #49899: [XLA:CPU] Do not offload reduce-window with base dilation to YNNPACK

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49899

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn` checked `base_dilation` only for window dimensions with `size > 1` or `stride > 1`. A dimension with window size 1 and stride 1 but `base_dilation = 2` passed the check, and `DefineReduceWindowOp` in the YNNPACK emitter never looks at base dilation, so it computed the undilated reduction and wrote it into the (larger) dilated output buffer. Silent wrong result, no error.

This change moves the base dilation check in front of the `size > 1 || stride > 1` block so it applies to every window dimension. Such reduce-windows now stay on the regular CPU emitter, which handles base dilation correctly. The window dilation and window reversal checks stay where they were, both are no-ops on a size 1 window.

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #48714. `LIBRARY_FUSION_TYPE_REDUCE` is enabled by default, so any CPU `reduce-window` with `lhs_dilate` on a size 1 / stride 1 dimension and at least 4096 elements returned wrong values. Reachable from plain `lax.reduce_window(..., base_dilation=...)` in JAX.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

- `YnnReduceTest.ReduceWindowWithBaseDilationIsNotFused` in `xla/backends/cpu/transforms/ynn_matcher_test.cc` compiles the module from the issue (`f32[64,128]`, `window={size=2x1 stride=2x1 lhs_dilate=1x2}`, max), checks that no `__ynn_fusion` is created, and compares the result against the interpreter with an exact error spec. The fixture gets the interpreter reference mixin for that.

Fails without the fix (fusion present, 8159 of 8160 elements wrong) and passes with it:

```
bazel test //xla/backends/cpu/transforms:ynn_matcher_test_cpu //xla/backends/cpu/tests:ynn_fusion_test_cpu //xla/tests:reduce_window_test_cpu
```

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

The new test runs the module on CPU and compares with the interpreter. The existing YNNPACK fusion and reduce-window test targets above still pass.
